Antibiotics should not be administered to patients who have received oral or parenteral antibiotics within 14 days prior to cholera vaccination, as these agents may interfere with the vaccine strain's activity. 2. Cefpodoxime can increase the levels or effects of choline magnesium trisalicylate due to competition for renal tubular clearance by acidic (anionic) drugs. This interaction is considered minor, but its clinical significance is unknown. Close monitoring is advised. 3. Cimetidine decreases the levels or effects of cefpodoxime by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution and monitor closely. 4. Clarithromycin reduces the effects of cefpodoxime through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 5. Bacteriostatic agents, such as clarithromycin, may inhibit the effects of bactericidal agents like cefpodoxime. Monitor closely. 6. Administer cefpodoxime at least 2 hours before or several hours after didanosine oral solution or chewable tablet administration. Monitor closely. 9. Cefpodoxime increases the levels or effects of willow bark by competing for renal tubular clearance with acidic (anionic) drugs. This interaction is considered minor, but its clinical significance is unknown. 50. Cefpodoxime is bactericidal against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. It inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis by binding to one or more penicillin-binding proteins, leading to bacterial lysis as cell-wall assembly is arrested while cell-wall autolytic enzymes remain active. 51. Cefpodoxime has a bioavailability of 50% and is acid-stable. It reaches peak plasma levels within 1 hour and is well-distributed into tissues, including the lungs and tonsils, and penetrates pleural fluid. It is 18–23% protein-bound, metabolized in the liver to an active metabolite, and has a half-life of 2–3 hours, which is prolonged in renal impairment. It is excreted primarily in the urine (80% as unchanged drug) within 24 hours. 52. Cefpodoxime is used to treat a wide variety of bacterial infections. It is a cephalosporin antibiotic and is effective only against bacterial infections, not viral infections like the common cold or flu. 53. Medications that reduce or block stomach acid, such as proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), H2 blockers, or antacids, may reduce cefpodoxime absorption, making it less effective. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for safe use of these medications with cefpodoxime. 54. Take cefpodoxime at evenly spaced intervals for the best effect. Complete the full prescribed course, even if symptoms improve after a few days. 55. Common side effects include diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, and headache. Rarely, it may cause a severe intestinal condition due to Clostridioides difficile, which can occur during or weeks to months after treatment. Prolonged or repeated use may result in oral thrush or a new vaginal yeast infection. 56. Serious allergic reactions to cefpodoxime are rare. However, use caution in patients with a history of penicillin or beta-lactam allergies, especially IgE-mediated reactions like angioedema, anaphylaxis, or urticaria. 57. Some dosage forms may contain benzyl alcohol derivatives, which are associated with potentially fatal toxicity (gasping syndrome) in neonates. Avoid or use with caution in neonates. 58. During pregnancy, cefpodoxime should be used only when clearly needed. It passes into breast milk in low concentrations and may have undesirable effects on nursing infants. 59. Cefpodoxime may interfere with certain lab tests, such as Coombs' test or urine glucose tests, potentially causing false results. 60. Store cefpodoxime tablets at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Refrigerate the suspension but do not freeze it. Discard unused suspension after 14 days.
